nodes.title: Moses Retells the Journey
nodes.summary: On the plains of Moab, Moses preaches the past: the failure at Kadesh, the wilderness years, the first victories — and warns the new generation that their God is a consuming fire who tolerates no idols. Deuteronomy is the Torah as sermon.

prerequisites.reason: Moses is addressing the new generation censused on these same plains of Moab.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses spends four chapters retelling a story most of his hearers were too young to remember. Why does he treat remembering as a survival skill for faith, and what practices help you keep hold of what God has done before you forget it?
assessment_questions: What failure at Kadesh does Moses retell, and what did it cost the previous generation?

Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb they saw no form of God, only heard a voice, and must therefore make no carved image. What is the connection between how God revealed himself and how he insists on being worshiped?
Moses warns against forgetting slowly, not only rebelling suddenly. What do you quietly rely on for security that could take God's place, and how would you catch that drift early?

teaching_concepts.concept: Faithful in covenant, just in consequence
teaching_concepts.explanation: God keeps his promise of the land while still judging the generation that refused to trust him, so his faithfulness never cancels his justice.
Moses insists the commands be kept in the heart and passed to children, because faith that is never rehearsed and never taught dies in one generation.
Because Israel heard a voice and saw no form at Horeb, any attempt to reduce God to an object misrepresents who he is.
The spies' generation had all the information and still refused to trust, showing that faith turns on trust in God's character rather than on evidence alone.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Moses retells the wilderness story to a generation that did not live it, and summarize the warning of Deuteronomy 4 against idols in your own words.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 4:9 commands Israel to remember what they saw and to teach it to their children. Within Moses' sermon, what work is all this remembering meant to do?
options: It preserves an accurate record for the nation's archives
It earns the next generation the credit their parents forfeited
It keeps trust alive where their parents' trust collapsed
It guarantees the coming conquest by rehearsing the old victories
comprehension_check.why: Moses ties memory to loyalty: the story is retold so the children hold to the God their parents doubted at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 4:9).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 4:9 again, right after the retelling of Horeb. Notice who the remembering is for.

comprehension_check.question: At Horeb Israel heard a voice out of the fire and saw no shape. Why does Moses build the idol ban on that detail in Deuteronomy 4:15-16?
options: An image would misrepresent the God who spoke there
Seeing is a less reliable way of knowing than hearing
The fire made any likeness too dangerous to attempt
Israel might mistake their own carvings for Canaan's gods
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 4:12 stresses that Israel received words and saw no form, so a shape would claim to show what God did not reveal.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 4:12-16 again. Notice what Israel received at Horeb and what they did not.

nodes.title: The Shema: Love the LORD Your God
nodes.summary: The Ten Commandments restated, then the center of Israel's faith: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart.' Jesus called this the greatest commandment; these chapters are also where he draws all three answers to the tempter in the wilderness.

prerequisites.reason: This is Sinai preached to the next generation; the Ten Words are restated, not introduced.

connections.reason: All three of Jesus' replies to Satan in the wilderness are quotations from Deuteronomy 6-8.
Jesus names the Shema as the first and greatest commandment.

nodes.discussion_prompt: The command at the center of these chapters is to love God with all your heart, soul, and strength. What does it mean for love to be commanded at all, and what would loving God with everything you have change about an ordinary Tuesday for you?
assessment_questions: What does the Shema declare about God, and what does Moses tell parents to do with these words at home and on the road?
Moses warns that the real danger will come after Israel eats and is satisfied in the land. Why does prosperity threaten their memory of God more than hardship did?
Jesus answered temptation with this section's words: man does not live by bread alone. Which appetite in your life most needs that sentence spoken over it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The commandments open with the God who brought Israel out of slavery, so obedience is a response to rescue rather than a way of earning it.
Israel's central confession is that the LORD is one and is to be loved with heart, soul, and strength, making whole-person devotion the core of the covenant.
The commands are to be talked about at home, on the road, at bedtime and morning, so ordinary family conversation becomes the main carrier of faith.
Moses warns that full stomachs and fine houses make people forget the God who provided them, so gratitude has to be practiced deliberately.

nodes.completion_criteria: Recite or paraphrase the Shema, and explain why Moses ties loving God to teaching children and to remembering him in prosperity.

comprehension_check.question: Before any command is given, Deuteronomy 5:6 names God as the one who brought Israel out of slavery. What does that opening establish about the law?
options: Obedience earns the favor God is offering Israel
Obedience answers a rescue that has already happened
Obedience repays a debt Israel owes for Egypt
Obedience completes a rescue that is still unfinished
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 5:6 puts redemption before command, so the law is given to a people God has already saved.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 5:6 again. Notice what God has already done before the first command arrives.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 6:4-7 stands at the center of Israel's faith. What do these verses make the covenant's core demand?
options: Faithful recitation of the words at set times
Complete separation from all the surrounding peoples
Exact obedience to each of the ten commands
Undivided love carried into every corner of life
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 6:5 calls for love with all the heart, soul, and strength, making whole-person devotion the covenant's center.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 6:4-7 again. Notice which single verb the commands gather around.

nodes.title: Worship in the Land: One Altar, Festivals, and Release
nodes.summary: The covenant code opens where the Shema pointed: one God will be worshiped at one chosen place, on his own terms, and every rival shrine and homemade cult must go. From there the code moves through the tests of enticing prophets and kin, the clean and unclean table, and a tithe that becomes a feast before the LORD. The rhythm of release follows, debts canceled and slaves freed in the seventh year with open-handedness commanded, and the section closes with the pilgrim festivals, all Israel traveling to appear before God, each bringing what his blessing allows.

prerequisites.reason: The statutes unpack the Shema — many scholars read chapters 12-26 as the Ten Commandments expanded in order.

nodes.discussion_prompt: This worship code keeps commanding joy: households told to rejoice before the LORD at the altar, at the tithe feast, and at the festivals, with servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows pulled into the celebration. What picture of worship is being painted when joy is legislated and the guest list is that wide, and how does it compare with yours?
assessment_questions: What does Deuteronomy 12:2-7 tell Israel to do about the existing shrines in the land, and where is worship to happen instead?

Deuteronomy 15 concedes that poverty will persist in the land, yet still commands lending freely and giving without a grudging heart. What understanding of ownership and blessing sits underneath a law like that?

Deuteronomy 16:17 measures each worshiper's festival gift by how the LORD has blessed him. If your giving this year were measured by that standard, blessing received against hand opened, what would it show, and what would you change first?

teaching_concepts.concept: One altar against a thousand shrines
teaching_concepts.explanation: Centralizing worship at the chosen place guards Israel from absorbing Canaan's cults and keeps the one God from being reimagined locally, unity of worship protecting truth of worship.
Chapter 12 closes by warning against everyone worshiping as he personally sees fit, making revelation rather than preference the rule of approach to God.
The seventh-year cancellation of debts and freeing of servants translates Israel's own rescue from Egypt into policy, generosity commanded because redemption was received.
Three annual pilgrimages gather the scattered tribes to one place to rehearse the exodus and the harvests together, so Israel's identity is renewed by shared, scheduled joy.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the code begins with the demand for one place of worship, and describe how the release year and the festivals each turn Israel's redemption from Egypt into practice.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 12 orders Canaan's shrines destroyed and worship gathered to the one place the LORD will choose. What is this law protecting?
options: The revenue a single sanctuary would concentrate for the priests
The purity of Israel's worship from the pull of local cults
The holy site itself, since God can be present only there
The land's peace, by ending rivalry between tribal shrines
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 12:4 and 12:30-31 give the reason: Israel must not serve the LORD in the ways the nations served their gods, so the chosen place guards the covenant.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 12:29-31 at the chapter's end. Notice what Israel is warned against asking about the nations' worship.

comprehension_check.question: Chapter 15 commands open hands toward the poor and freed servants sent away loaded with gifts. Where does the law anchor that demand?
options: In the shame a stingy household would bring on its town
In a bargain where generosity purchases the LORD's continued blessing
In the assurance that poverty is about to disappear
In Israel's own memory of being freed and provided for
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 15:15 grounds the command in Israel's own story of slavery and redemption, which is why the freed servant leaves loaded with provisions.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 15:12-15. Notice the reason attached to the command about how a freed servant leaves.

nodes.title: Israel's Offices: Judge, King, Priest, Prophet
nodes.summary: In a few tight paragraphs the code constitutes a nation's public life: judges in every town charged to pursue justice without bribes or favoritism, a king permitted but stripped of the usual engines of royal power and set to daily reading of this law, priests and Levites given service in place of territory, and the promise of a prophet like Moses through whom God will keep speaking. Every office faces the same direction, standing under the covenant word rather than over it, and even prophecy is given a test to keep it honest.

prerequisites.reason: The offices law continues the same covenant code, turning from worship to the nation's institutions.

connections.reason: Stephen cites Deuteronomy 18's 'prophet like Moses' promise of Jesus (Acts 7:37), as Peter does in Acts 3:22.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Israel's king is denied the tools ancient kings ran on, war horses, a harem of alliances, and heaped-up gold, and is assigned daily reading of the covenant instead. What is this law trying to make a ruler into, and what would its equivalent look like for the kinds of power you see up close?
assessment_questions: What is Israel's future king commanded to do with this law in Deuteronomy 17:18-20, and what three things is he forbidden to multiply?
Judges, king, priests, and prophet are each defined by limits and duties before God. Taken together, what vision of power do the four offices add up to?

Deuteronomy 18:21-22 anticipates the question of how to tell a true word from a false one and gives Israel a test. Where do you currently take in voices claiming authority, and what tests do you actually apply before trusting them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The section opens by seating courts in every town and binding them to impartiality, making everyday local justice the ground the other offices stand on.

The law strips the throne of harem, treasury, and war machine and chains it to a handwritten copy of the covenant, an inversion of ancient kingship that Israel's later story keeps measuring its kings against.
Priests and Levites live from the offerings and hold no tribal territory, their support woven into worship so that the teachers of the law depend on the people they teach.
God promises to keep speaking through a prophet he will raise up, with listening as the command and fulfillment as the test, a promise the New Testament applies to Jesus.

nodes.completion_criteria: List the four offices of this section with the main limit or duty attached to each, and explain what the promise of a prophet like Moses adds to Israel's future.

comprehension_check.question: The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14-20 forbids the usual royal accumulations and prescribes daily reading instead. What is the design?
options: A ruler kept humble and governed by the covenant
A throne kept weak so that priests hold the real power
A test proving whether Israel deserves a king at all
A king made in the image of the nations' emperors
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 17:19-20 gives the aim: daily reading so the king learns to fear the LORD and stays level with his brothers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 17:16-20. Notice what the king is denied, what he must produce by hand, and what the reading is said to prevent.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 18:9-22 bans the nations' divination and then promises a prophet like Moses. How do the ban and the promise fit together?
options: Israel may use only divination its own priests supervise
Israel must wait without revelation until the prophet arrives
God's own speech replaces the nations' hidden arts
Israel replaces the pagan seers with a hereditary office
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 18:14-15 draws the contrast itself: the dispossessed nations listen to diviners, while Israel will listen to the prophet the LORD raises up.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 18:14-18. Notice the word about listening that links what the nations do with what Israel must do.

nodes.title: Life Together: Justice, Warfare, Family, and Mercy
nodes.summary: The code now walks through common life: cities of refuge and the law of witnesses, rules that restrain war, and a dense weave of household and neighbor cases, marriage wronged, property strayed, wages withheld, gleanings left for the poor. Under the variety runs one refrain, Israel told again and again to remember its own slavery, so that mercy to the vulnerable becomes the nation's signature. The code then closes in liturgy: firstfruits offered with the wandering-Aramean confession, and Israel and the LORD each declaring the other their own.

prerequisites.reason: The communal law completes the code after the nation's offices are established.

nodes.discussion_prompt: These chapters legislate small mercies, a cloak returned by sunset, wages paid the same day, sheaves left where they fell, a mother bird let go. Why do you think a national law code descends to details this small, and which small structural mercy could you build into your own routines?
assessment_questions: According to Deuteronomy 24:17-22, which three groups keep reappearing in these protections, and what memory is Israel told to attach to them?

The code ends its long run of cases with the firstfruits liturgy and the mutual declarations of Deuteronomy 26:16-19. What does closing hundreds of laws with worship and belonging say about what all the laws were for?

The gleaning law provides for the poor by telling owners what to leave rather than what to hand out. What is the difference between those two kinds of giving, and where could you leave an edge of your field this month?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Refuge cities, multiple witnesses, and proportionate penalties build restraint into the system itself, so the innocent are protected from mobs and courts alike.
Chapter 20 and its companions put limits, exemptions, and obligations around warfare, refusing to let necessity or victory suspend Israel's accountability to God.
The code keeps grounding protections for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow in Israel's own years as slaves, making compassion an act of remembering.
The code closes with gratitude spoken over a basket of firstfruits and covenant declarations exchanged, revealing obedience as the shape of a relationship rather than a ledger.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe three concrete protections this section builds for the vulnerable and the memory each is tied to, and explain how chapter 26 turns the whole code into covenant commitment.

comprehension_check.question: Laws about cloaks, wages, and gleanings keep citing Israel's years in Egypt. What work is that memory doing in the code?
options: It warns that disobedience could send Israel back to slavery
It ranks the redeemed nation above the foreigners among them
It dates the laws to the generation that left Egypt
It makes Israel's own rescue the measure of its mercy
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 24:18 attaches the reason directly to the command: Israel remembers slavery and redemption, and treats the vulnerable accordingly.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 24:17-22. Notice the sentence that repeats after the commands and what it asks Israel to recall.

comprehension_check.question: After chapters of case law, the code ends in Deuteronomy 26 with a confession over firstfruits and mutual declarations. What does the ending reveal?
options: The rituals of chapter 26 outrank the case laws before them
The laws aim at a people bound to God in love
The whole code was recited yearly at the firstfruits ceremony
The closing confession earns blessings the laws alone could not
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 26:17-19 seals the code with a mutual pledge, Israel declaring the LORD its God and the LORD declaring Israel his treasured people.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 26:16-19. Notice who makes a declaration in these verses and what each party declares.

nodes.title: Blessing, Curse, and the Choice of Life
nodes.summary: Covenant blessings for obedience, devastating curses for rebellion — up to and including exile — and then, astonishingly, a promise beyond the curse: God will circumcise hearts and bring his scattered people home. 'Choose life.' The prophets and Paul both build on these chapters.

prerequisites.reason: The blessings and curses are the sanctions attached to the code just given — the covenant's signature page.

connections.reason: 'Cursed is everyone hanged on a tree' (Deut 21) and the curse of the law (Deut 27) anchor Galatians 3.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30's 'the word is near you' as the voice of righteousness by faith.
The exile to Babylon is the Deuteronomy 28 curse executed in history.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses lays out blessing and curse, predicts that Israel will fail, and then promises that God will circumcise their hearts so they can finally love him. What does that sequence suggest about where the power to obey actually comes from, and what would asking God for a changed heart mean for you?
assessment_questions: What two paths does Moses set before Israel at the end of chapter 30, and what does he beg them to choose?
Before Israel has even entered the land, chapter 30 already assumes exile and promises return. What does it mean that restoration is written into the covenant from the very start?
Moses says the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so obedience is within reach. Which choice in front of you right now is really a choice between life and death in slow motion?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The blessings and curses declare that covenant choices carry real outcomes, up to and including exile from the land.
The covenant addresses the whole nation while summoning each Israelite to choose, so no one can hide inside the crowd or stand outside the community.
God promises to gather his scattered people when they return to him, so failure is anticipated and mercy is already prepared on the far side of it.
Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God himself will change hearts so that love for him becomes possible, pointing forward to inward renewal rather than mere rule-keeping.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the choice Moses sets before Israel in Deuteronomy 30, and describe what the promise of a circumcised heart adds to the blessings and curses.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 30:1-3 promises return and regathering, placed directly after the curse chapters. What does that placement reveal?
options: The covenant already carries mercy for its own breaking
The curses were warnings God never intended to enforce
Israel will avoid exile if this generation stays faithful
Repentance can cancel the curse before it ever lands
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 30:1 assumes the curse will actually fall and still promises regathering beyond it, so mercy is written into the covenant from the start.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 30:1-3 again. Notice which events Moses treats as certain before the return is promised.

comprehension_check.question: The command is to love God with the whole heart, yet Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that the LORD himself will circumcise Israel's heart. What does that promise admit?
options: Wholehearted love is a goal reached by steady practice
Covenant obedience requires a change only God can give
God rewards the love Israel first works up itself
Israel's failure came from laws that asked too much
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 30:6 has God performing the circumcision so that love for him follows, locating the deepest obedience in his gift.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 30:6 again. Notice who performs the circumcising and what it is meant to produce.

nodes.title: The Death of Moses
nodes.summary: Moses commissions Joshua, teaches Israel a witness-song predicting their future failure and God's faithfulness, blesses the tribes, and dies on Mount Nebo overlooking a land he will never enter. 'No prophet like him has arisen since' — a deliberate cliffhanger the New Testament answers.

prerequisites.reason: Moses' song and death are the covenant ceremony's conclusion.

connections.reason: Moses finally stands in the promised land at the Transfiguration, beside the prophet greater than he.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses climbs Nebo, sees the land he spent forty years walking toward, and dies without entering it. What do these chapters say about a faithful life that ends with promises still open, and how does that change what you would count as a successful life?
assessment_questions: Where does Moses die, who buries him, and what does the closing tribute say made him unlike any prophet since?
God has Moses teach Israel a song that predicts their unfaithfulness before it happens. Why would God give a people a witness-song against themselves?

Moses tells Joshua that the LORD goes before him and will never leave him or forsake him. What task feels too big for you right now, and how would taking that promise seriously change the way you step into it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses commissions Joshua before he dies, showing that the covenant work continues on God's faithfulness rather than on any one leader.

teaching_concepts.concept: The word made public and memorable
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses has the law written down and read aloud to everyone, so covenant faith is preserved as a shared possession that each generation can hear.
The Song of Moses announces both Israel's future failure and God's faithfulness, standing as a testimony the people carry in their own mouths.

teaching_concepts.concept: Even the greatest servant is mortal
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses dies with the promise still ahead of him, leaving a deliberate cliffhanger that keeps hope fixed on God and on the prophet still to come.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the death of Moses on Nebo, and explain what the Song of Moses and Joshua's commissioning each say about God's faithfulness beyond one leader's life.

comprehension_check.question: In Deuteronomy 31:16-21 God predicts Israel's apostasy before Moses even dies, then commissions a song about it. What does this pairing say about the covenant's future?
options: The covenant will lapse once the apostasy arrives
The next generation may yet escape the prediction
God regrets the covenant he made at Horeb
Israel's coming failure is foreseen and already answered
comprehension_check.why: In Deuteronomy 31:21 God commissions the song precisely because he knows what Israel will do, so provision outruns the failure.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 31:19-21 again. Notice when the song is written relative to the sin it concerns.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy ends with Moses dead outside the land and a note in Deuteronomy 34:10 that no prophet like him has risen. What kind of ending is that?
options: A closed ending, the Torah's story finished at Moses' grave
An open ending that keeps Israel waiting on God's promise
A cautionary ending about trusting any single human leader
A quiet ending meant to honor Moses above the law
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 34:4 shows the promise still ahead and Deuteronomy 34:10 leaves the prophet's place unfilled, so the book closes leaning forward.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 34:4 and 34:10 together. Notice what Moses sees and what the final verses say has not yet come.
